clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive low-GGT cholestasis caused by ATP8B1 mutations encoding FIC1, a canalicular aminophospholipid flippase; serum bile acids are markedly raised while GGT is characteristically low or normal.

The hallmark distinguishing PFIC1 from PFIC2 is prominent extrahepatic disease, reflecting FIC1 expression beyond the liver: watery secretory diarrhoea, pancreatitis, sensorineural hearing loss and a raised sweat chloride.
Intractable pruritus is often severe and out of proportion to the degree of jaundice, dominating quality of life and driving management.
Growth failure and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency are prominent and frequently precede overt hepatic decompensation.
Coarse, granular canalicular bile (Byler bile) on electron microscopy is a characteristic ultrastructural clue.

Allelic disorders form a spectrum: benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis type 1 (BRIC1) is a milder, episodic phenotype, and ATP8B1 variants also contribute to intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Surgical biliary diversion can relieve pruritus and may slow hepatic progression in selected children.
Liver transplantation corrects the hepatic disease but does not resolve extrahepatic features and may worsen diarrhoea and produce steatosis of the graft.
reference.pathophysiology: ATP8B1 encodes FIC1, a P4-type ATPase that flips aminophospholipids, notably phosphatidylserine, from the outer to the inner leaflet of the canalicular membrane, preserving membrane asymmetry and protecting the hepatocyte apical surface from the detergent action of luminal bile salts. Loss of FIC1 function destabilises the canalicular membrane and impairs bile salt secretion, in part through disturbed farnesoid X receptor signalling and secondary downregulation of the bile salt export pump, so cytotoxic bile acids accumulate within hepatocytes and drive progressive cholestatic injury and fibrosis. Because FIC1 is also expressed in cholangiocytes, enterocytes, pancreatic and airway epithelia and the cochlea, deficiency produces the characteristic extrahepatic manifestations of secretory diarrhoea, pancreatitis, elevated sweat electrolytes and sensorineural deafness that set this subtype apart from the liver-restricted transporter defects.
additionalDifferentials: PFIC type 2 (ABCB11/BSEP deficiency) — also low GGT but liver-restricted, no diarrhoea or deafness

Coagulopathy and bleeding from vitamin K malabsorption
Progression to cirrhosis with portal hypertension

reference.prognosis: Untreated disease progresses to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease during childhood, though biliary diversion can relieve pruritus and slow progression in some. Extrahepatic features persist and diarrhoea and graft steatosis may worsen after transplantation.
pitfalls: Interpreting a low or normal GGT as reassuring or as evidence against significant cholestasis
Expecting liver transplantation to cure the extrahepatic manifestations
Overlooking sensorineural hearing loss or pancreatitis as related features
Misattributing the secretory diarrhoea to an unrelated functional or infective cause
